lessons.title: Turn a product description into a client-ready campaign brief with AI
lessons.summary: Use Claude or ChatGPT to transform a rough product description into a structured campaign brief covering audience, positioning, and channels — in minutes instead of a full afternoon.
lessons.goal: Produce a complete, structured campaign brief from a short product description using one well-built prompt.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every downstream asset — ads, landing pages, emails, social posts — depends on a solid brief, but writing one from scratch eats half a day and gets skipped under deadline pressure. A fast, structured first-draft brief gives you a clear foundation to build creative from instead of guessing at audience and message as you go, and gives clients or stakeholders something concrete to react to early.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A short product or service description — your own or a client's. A few sentences of raw notes is enough; you don't need a finished description.
steps: Gather whatever you already know about the product: what it is, who buys it, what it costs, and any existing notes on competitors or positioning.
Paste the raw product description into the prompt below, even if it's messy or incomplete.
State the campaign's real goal (awareness, leads, sales, launch) — this single word changes every section of a good brief.
Run the prompt and read the brief section by section, checking labeled assumptions against what you actually know.
Correct or confirm each assumption directly in the chat rather than starting over.
Fill in any section the AI left as a placeholder because you didn't originally give it that information.
Save the finished brief as the reference document for every later prompt in this campaign (ad angles, landing page, emails).
lessons.prompt:
You are a senior marketing strategist writing a campaign brief for an internal team. Use only the information in the product description below. Where you need to make an assumption (audience, price point, competitors, etc.), state it clearly as an assumption, not as fact, and flag it with [ASSUMPTION].

Product description: [PASTE YOUR RAW PRODUCT DESCRIPTION]
Campaign goal: [e.g. drive trial sign-ups / launch awareness / holiday sales]
Budget or scale (if known): [e.g. small paid social test / full multi-channel launch]

Produce a campaign brief with these sections:
1. Product Summary (2-3 sentences)
2. Target Audience(s) — 1-3 specific segments, not "everyone"
3. Core Problem / Pain Point each segment has
4. Positioning Statement (one sentence: for [audience], [product] is the [category] that [benefit], unlike [alternative])
5. Key Message (the one thing every asset should communicate)
6. Supporting Proof Points (from the description only — do not invent stats or claims)
7. Recommended Primary Channels and why
8. Tone and Voice guidance
9. Success Metric for this campaign

Keep it under 400 words. Use headers, not paragraphs of prose.
lessons.explanation: Telling the model to flag assumptions instead of presenting them as fact is the single most important line in this prompt — it stops a confident-sounding but wrong audience or positioning statement from quietly becoming the foundation of an entire campaign. Naming the campaign goal up front changes what a good brief looks like (an awareness brief and a sales brief should not read the same), and forcing proof points to come only from the description prevents the model from inventing a stat or claim you didn't provide and can't back up.
lessons.example:
Input: "A subscription box for home baristas — monthly shipment of freshly roasted specialty coffee beans from a different small farm each month, plus a tasting card. $28/month, cancel anytime." Campaign goal: drive trial sign-ups.

Output: a brief that names 2-3 segments (e.g. home coffee enthusiasts upgrading from supermarket beans, gift-buyers), flags audience income level as [ASSUMPTION] rather than stating it as fact, proposes a positioning statement built only from the given details, and recommends channels suited to trial sign-ups rather than brand awareness.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, run this prompt with a real product or service you currently market. Correct at least one flagged assumption using information you actually have.
lessons.expectedResult: A one-page brief with no unlabeled invented facts, where every section traces back either to your input or to a clearly marked assumption you can now confirm or correct.
commonMistakes: Pasting a polished product description instead of raw notes, which produces a generic brief instead of one grounded in your actual knowledge.
Skipping the campaign goal field, which causes the model to default to a generic 'brand awareness' brief that doesn't match what you actually need.
Accepting flagged assumptions without checking them, so incorrect guesses about audience or price quietly become the base of the whole campaign.
Treating the first output as final instead of as a first draft to correct and fill in.
lessons.proTip: Keep this brief as a pinned reference (a Claude Project or a ChatGPT pinned chat) so every later prompt in the campaign — ad angles, landing page, emails — can reference it directly instead of re-explaining the product each time.

lessons.title: Turn a product brief into 20 distinct ad angles
lessons.summary: Generate a wide, genuinely varied set of ad angles from one brief so you test real differences in message, not twenty rewordings of the same idea.
lessons.goal: Produce 20 distinct ad angles from a single campaign brief, grouped by strategic approach rather than by wording.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most 'brainstorm 20 ideas' prompts return the same angle worded twenty different ways, which wastes testing budget on redundant variants that all win or lose together. Structuring the request around distinct psychological and strategic approaches — not just different phrasing — gives you a testing set that actually tells you which message works.
steps: Have your campaign brief (or a short product description plus audience) ready to paste in.
Ask for angles grouped by strategic category, not a flat list of 20 — this is what forces real variety.
Run the prompt and scan the category headers first, before reading individual angles, to confirm the categories themselves are genuinely different.
Flag any category that's really a duplicate of another and ask the model to replace it.
Pick your top 5-8 angles across at least 4 different categories, not all from one category, to build a real test.
Ask for a one-line ad hook for each shortlisted angle so you have something testable, not just a theme.
lessons.prompt:
You are a direct-response advertising strategist. Based on the campaign brief below, generate 20 distinct ad angles for [PRODUCT NAME], grouped into these 5 categories (4 angles each):
1. Pain/problem-led (lead with the frustration the product solves)
2. Outcome/aspiration-led (lead with the result or transformation)
3. Social proof/authority-led (lead with trust, numbers, or expertise)
4. Objection-handling (lead with the reason a skeptical buyer hasn't bought yet)
5. Curiosity/contrarian (lead with an unexpected claim or against-the-grain take)

For each angle, give: a one-line ad hook (under 12 words) and a one-sentence explanation of the psychology behind it. Do not repeat the same core idea across categories — each of the 20 should be a genuinely different reason to buy, not a rewording.

Campaign brief: [PASTE BRIEF OR PRODUCT DESCRIPTION + AUDIENCE]
lessons.explanation: The category structure is what prevents redundancy: it's far harder for a model to accidentally produce 20 near-duplicates when it's forced to hit five conceptually different buying psychologies four times each. Requiring a one-sentence 'why this works' per angle also makes weak or generic angles easy to spot — if the explanation could apply to any product, the angle isn't specific enough to test.
lessons.example:
Input: brief for a project management tool for small agencies.

Output: 20 angles across the five categories — e.g. pain-led: "Stop losing billable hours to status update emails"; outcome-led: "Ship client work a week faster, every sprint"; objection-handling: "No setup team required — live in one afternoon" — each with a distinct psychological rationale, not four versions of the same headline.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, run this prompt using a real brief or product description. Shortlist 6 angles spanning at least 4 of the 5 categories.
lessons.expectedResult: A 20-angle list where reading the category headers alone tells you the strategic variety exists, and your 6-angle shortlist represents genuinely different reasons to buy, not restated headlines.
commonMistakes: Asking for '20 ad angles' with no category structure, which reliably produces near-duplicate wording.
Shortlisting all your favorites from one category, which defeats the purpose of testing different psychological approaches.
Accepting vague hooks ("Try it today!") without asking for the specific pain, outcome, or proof behind each one.
Skipping the brief and prompting from memory of the product, which pulls the model toward generic angles instead of ones grounded in your actual audience.
lessons.proTip: Run this same prompt again later in the campaign with 'avoid these angles: [list already-tested angles]' to keep generating genuinely new territory instead of circling back to the same five ideas.

lessons.title: Generate and systematically improve ad copy variants
lessons.summary: Turn one winning ad angle into a disciplined set of testable variants, then use structured critique prompts to improve the weak ones instead of guessing at rewrites.
lessons.goal: Produce a controlled set of ad copy variants for one angle, then use a critique-and-revise loop to strengthen the weakest ones.
lessons.whyItMatters: Random variant generation produces copy that differs in wording but not in what's actually being tested, which makes results impossible to interpret. Varying one element at a time — and using the model to critique its own output against real ad-copy criteria — gets you a test you can actually learn from, and copy that improves round over round instead of drifting.
steps: Pick one ad angle and platform (e.g. Meta feed ad, Google search ad) — variants should stay within one platform's format and length limits.
Ask for variants that isolate one variable at a time: hook, length, or call-to-action — not everything changed at once.
Generate 5-6 variants for the chosen variable.
Run a second prompt asking the model to critique each variant against specific ad-copy criteria (clarity, specificity, CTA strength) and score them.
Ask it to rewrite only the lowest-scoring 2-3 variants, addressing the specific weakness named in the critique.
Do a final human pass: read every variant aloud and cut anything that still sounds like ad-copy filler.
lessons.prompt:
You are an ad copywriter. Below is one ad angle and platform. Generate 6 variants that test only the HOOK (opening line) while keeping the body and CTA identical. Each hook must be under [X] characters for [platform].

Angle: [PASTE ANGLE FROM PREVIOUS LESSON]
Platform: [e.g. Meta feed ad, Google search headline]
Body copy (keep identical across all variants): [PASTE BODY COPY]
CTA (keep identical): [e.g. "Start your free trial"]

Then, for each variant, score it 1-5 on: (a) specificity — does it name a concrete detail, not a vague claim, (b) clarity — is the offer instantly understandable, (c) pattern interrupt — would it stop a scroll. List the score and one sentence of reasoning per variant. Finally, rewrite only the two lowest-scoring hooks, explicitly fixing the weakness you identified.
lessons.explanation: Isolating one variable (the hook) while holding body and CTA constant is what makes a test result mean something — if three elements change at once, a win or loss can't be attributed to anything specific. Asking for scored critique against named criteria, rather than an open-ended 'make it better,' forces the model to justify what's weak instead of just producing more copy, and the targeted rewrite step means you fix the actual named problem instead of generating six fresh options and hoping one is better.
lessons.example:
Input: angle "Stop losing billable hours to status update emails," Meta feed ad, CTA "Start your free trial."

Output: 6 hook variants (e.g. a question hook, a stat-style hook, a direct-address hook), each scored on specificity/clarity/pattern-interrupt with one-line reasoning, and a rewritten version of the two weakest — for instance a vague hook like "Save time on your projects" rewritten to name the specific behavior it's replacing.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, run this prompt on a real ad angle. Identify which variant you'd actually run first and why, based on the scores given.
lessons.expectedResult: Six hook variants that differ in one dimension only, a scored breakdown you can defend to a client or teammate, and two improved rewrites that fix a specifically named weakness.
commonMistakes: Letting the model change the body copy or CTA between variants, which makes it impossible to tell what a test result actually measured.
Accepting scores without reading the one-sentence reasoning, which is where the actually useful feedback lives.
Asking for 'better' copy with no named criteria, producing rewrites that are different but not necessarily stronger.
Running only one round of critique-and-revise when a second pass on the same weak variant often gets a bigger improvement than a fresh batch.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running doc of which hook types (question, stat, direct-address, pattern-interrupt) actually won in past tests, and paste that history into future prompts so new variants build on what's already worked for your audience instead of starting blind each time.

lessons.title: Write and build landing-page copy that converts, from brief to working page
lessons.summary: Turn your campaign brief and winning ad angle into structured landing-page copy, then use Codex to assemble it into a working page so copy and layout are tested together instead of copy alone.
lessons.goal: Produce section-by-section landing-page copy tied to a proven ad angle, and generate a working page from it.
lessons.whyItMatters: Landing-page copy that gets written in isolation from the ad that drove the click, or from the page layout it will actually sit in, routinely fails to convert even when each sentence reads well on its own. Writing copy explicitly matched to your ad's promise, structured by section, and then seeing it in an actual page layout catches mismatches — a weak headline, a CTA buried below the fold — before you spend on traffic.
lessons.beforeYouStart: The ad angle and hook you're driving traffic from, and your campaign brief from an earlier lesson.
steps: Identify the exact ad angle and hook that will drive traffic to this page — the page headline must match that promise, not restate the brand generically.
Draft the copy section by section (hero, problem, solution, proof, objections, CTA) with Claude or ChatGPT, keeping the ad-to-page promise consistent.
Write objection-handling copy for the 2-3 real reasons a qualified visitor wouldn't convert, not generic reassurance.
Review the full copy for message match against the ad hook before moving to layout.
Hand the finished copy to Codex with a request to build a single-page HTML layout implementing it, so you can see headline, hero, and CTA placement together.
Read the built page top to bottom as a first-time visitor would and note anywhere the promise from the ad isn't delivered within the first screen.
lessons.prompt:
You are a conversion copywriter. Write landing-page copy for [PRODUCT/OFFER] that a visitor will land on immediately after clicking an ad with this exact hook: [PASTE AD HOOK]. The headline must directly continue that promise — do not write a generic brand headline.

Campaign brief: [PASTE BRIEF]

Write these sections:
1. Hero: headline (under 10 words, continues the ad promise) + one-sentence subheadline + primary CTA button text
2. Problem (2-3 sentences naming the specific pain, matching the audience in the brief)
3. Solution (3-4 sentences, how it works, no jargon)
4. Proof (structure for 2-3 proof points — use [PLACEHOLDER] for any stat or testimonial you don't have yet, do not invent one)
5. Objection-handling (address the 2-3 most likely reasons this specific audience hesitates)
6. Final CTA section: one sentence of urgency or reassurance + CTA button text

Keep sentences short. No more than one adjective in a row. Write for a visitor who has 8 seconds to decide whether to keep reading.

---
Then, hand the finished copy to Codex with:
Build a single-page HTML landing page using this copy: [PASTE FINAL COPY]. Hero section at the top with headline, subheadline, and CTA button visible without scrolling. Sections in this order: problem, solution, proof, objections, final CTA. Simple, readable layout — no placeholder images needed, use the text as-is.
lessons.explanation: Anchoring the headline explicitly to the ad hook is the single fix for the most common landing-page failure: a visitor clicking a specific promise and landing on a generic 'Welcome to [Brand]' page, which reads as a bait-and-switch and tanks conversion. Requiring placeholders instead of invented stats or testimonials protects you from publishing a false claim. Handing the finished copy to Codex to build an actual page — rather than just a copy document — forces you to see the CTA placement and section order the way a real visitor will, which catches structural problems, like a strong headline undercut by a buried button, that copy alone never reveals.
lessons.example:
Ad hook: "Stop losing billable hours to status update emails."

Output hero headline: something like "Your team's status updates, automated — not chased." A generic brand-first headline ("Welcome to ProjectFlow") would be a clear message-match failure. The Codex build step then produces a working single-page HTML file you can actually scroll through, so you can confirm the headline, subheadline, and CTA button all appear together in the first screen before any traffic is sent.
lessons.exercise: In your own accounts, draft copy for a real offer tied to a real ad hook, then ask Codex to build a simple single-page layout from it. Check whether the CTA is visible without scrolling.
lessons.expectedResult: Section-by-section copy that reads as a direct continuation of the ad promise, and a working page where the headline, hero, and CTA are visible together in the first screen.
commonMistakes: Writing a landing page headline that restates the brand instead of continuing the specific promise the ad made, breaking message match.
Letting the model invent a testimonial or statistic instead of leaving a clearly marked placeholder.
Writing generic objection-handling copy ('we care about quality') instead of naming the specific hesitation this audience has.
Reviewing only the copy document and never checking how it actually lays out on a page, missing that the CTA ends up below the fold.
lessons.proTip: Keep the ad hook pinned at the top of every landing-page prompt for that campaign — the moment the hook and headline drift apart is usually the moment conversion rate drops, even if both individually read well.

lessons.title: Build a multi-email sequence from one core offer
lessons.summary: Turn a single offer into a coherent 5-email sequence with a distinct job for each email, instead of five emails that all pitch the same thing the same way.
lessons.goal: Produce a 5-email sequence where each email has a distinct strategic job and the sequence builds toward the offer instead of repeating it.
lessons.whyItMatters: The most common email sequence failure is five emails that are really the same pitch reworded, which trains subscribers to skim and unsubscribe. Assigning each email a specific job in the sequence — value, story, objection, urgency, close — produces a set that builds trust and moves someone toward a decision instead of just repeating an ask.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Your campaign brief and core offer details (what's being offered, price/terms, deadline if any).
steps: Define the single offer this whole sequence supports — one offer, not several, or the sequence loses focus.
Assign each email in the sequence one job: deliver value, tell a story/case, handle the top objection, create urgency, direct close.
Generate the sequence with the job for each email specified explicitly in the prompt, not left for the model to invent.
Check that only the value email and the close email mention the offer directly at length — earlier emails should reference it briefly, not repeat the full pitch.
Review subject lines together as a set — they should look like a sequence from the same sender, not five unrelated emails.
Ask for a shortened SMS or push-notification version of the urgency email if you're also using that channel.
lessons.prompt:
You are an email marketer writing a 5-email sequence for one offer. Do not repeat the full pitch in every email — each email has ONE job:
Email 1 (Value): teach something genuinely useful related to the problem this offer solves. Mention the offer in one sentence at the end only.
Email 2 (Story/Proof): a short case study or scenario showing the problem being solved.
Email 3 (Objection): directly name and answer the single biggest reason this audience hesitates to buy.
Email 4 (Urgency): a real reason to act now (deadline, limited spots, price change) — do not invent a fake scarcity claim if none exists.
Email 5 (Close): a short, direct final ask with a clear CTA and a one-line recap of the offer.

Offer: [PASTE OFFER DETAILS: WHAT, PRICE/TERMS, DEADLINE IF ANY]
Audience: [PASTE AUDIENCE FROM BRIEF]

For each email, write: subject line, preview text, and body (120-200 words). Keep the sender's voice consistent across all five. Flag with [NEEDS REAL DATA] anywhere you'd normally want a real stat or deadline I haven't given you.
lessons.explanation: Assigning one explicit job per email is what stops the sequence from collapsing into five versions of the same pitch — without it, the model defaults to restating the offer in every email because that's the safest generic choice. The instruction not to invent fake scarcity matters because false urgency claims (fake countdown timers, made-up limited spots) damage trust and, in some jurisdictions, create legal exposure; flagging where real data is needed keeps that risk visible instead of silently filled in.
lessons.example:
Offer: a $200-off early-bird price on a course, ending in 7 days.

Output: Email 1 teaches one real tip related to the course topic with a one-line offer mention at the end; Email 3 names the actual top objection (e.g. "I don't have time for a course right now") and answers it directly; Email 4 uses the real 7-day deadline rather than inventing a countdown; Email 5 is short, direct, and recaps price and deadline in one line.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, run this prompt with a real offer you're promoting. Confirm each email is doing its assigned job and not slipping into a full repeat pitch.
lessons.expectedResult: A 5-email sequence where an outside reader could name each email's specific job just from reading it, and no email past #2 repeats the full pitch.
commonMistakes: Letting every email restate the full offer at length, which is the default failure mode without explicit per-email jobs.
Inventing a fake deadline or scarcity claim when none actually exists.
Writing five unrelated subject lines that don't read as coming from the same sequence or sender.
Skipping the objection email because it feels negative, when it's usually the email that converts the most hesitant readers.
lessons.proTip: After sending, feed the open and click-through rates for each email back into a follow-up prompt asking the model to diagnose which specific email's job it may have failed at (e.g. low opens on Email 3 often means the subject line buried the objection instead of naming it).

lessons.title: Create a monthly social content calendar from your campaign themes
lessons.summary: Generate a full month of platform-appropriate social posts organized around a content mix, instead of a scattered list of disconnected post ideas.
lessons.goal: Produce a 30-day social content calendar with a defined content mix, platform-specific formatting, and no repeated post concepts.
lessons.whyItMatters: A month of social content built post-by-post drifts toward whatever's easiest to write that day — usually promotional posts — which fatigues an audience fast. Planning against a fixed content mix (value, engagement, promotion, proof) up front produces a calendar that actually holds attention over 30 days and gives you a defensible plan to show a client or manager before you start writing captions.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Your campaign brief, key themes/topics for the month, and which platforms you're posting to.
steps: Decide the content mix ratio you want (e.g. 40% value/education, 20% engagement/community, 20% proof/social proof, 20% promotion) before generating anything.
List 4-6 core themes or topics for the month so posts don't repeat the same idea.
Specify platforms and their format constraints (character limits, whether video/image is implied) so posts don't need reformatting later.
Generate the calendar with content-type and theme labeled for every post, not just the caption.
Scan the calendar for any two posts that make essentially the same point and ask for one to be replaced.
Pull out the week's promotional posts separately and check they don't cluster on consecutive days.
lessons.prompt:
You are a social media strategist. Build a 30-day content calendar for [PLATFORM(S)] following this content mix: [e.g. 40% value/education, 20% engagement, 20% proof, 20% promotion].

Themes for this month (rotate across these, don't repeat the same idea twice): [LIST 4-6 THEMES]
Brand voice: [PASTE FROM BRIEF]
Posting frequency: [e.g. 5 posts/week]

For each post give: date, content type (from the mix categories), theme, caption (platform-appropriate length), and a one-line visual/format note (e.g. carousel, short video, single image — describe the shot, do not generate the asset). Do not place two promotional posts within 3 days of each other. End with a short summary table counting posts per content-type to confirm the mix ratio was followed.
lessons.explanation: Fixing the content mix ratio before generating anything is what prevents the calendar from drifting toward all-promotion, which is the model's (and most marketers') default under time pressure. The closing summary table forces a self-check against the stated ratio, so a skewed calendar is caught immediately instead of discovered after a month of underperforming engagement. The rule against clustering promotional posts protects the value-first feel that keeps an audience from muting the account.
lessons.example:
Input: Instagram + LinkedIn, mix 40/20/20/20, themes: product tips, customer wins, industry trends, behind-the-scenes, 5 posts/week.

Output: a day-by-day table where, say, Monday is a value post on a product tip, Wednesday is an engagement post (a question to the audience), Friday is a proof post (a customer result), with promotional posts spaced across the month rather than bunched — plus a closing count confirming roughly 12 value / 6 engagement / 6 proof / 6 promotion posts across the 30 days.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, build a real 30-day calendar for one of your platforms. Verify in the summary table that the actual mix matches your intended ratio.
lessons.expectedResult: A full month of labeled, non-repetitive posts where the closing count confirms the content mix you specified, and no two promotional posts sit within 3 days of each other.
commonMistakes: Skipping the content mix ratio and letting the calendar default to mostly promotional posts.
Listing too few themes, which causes visible repetition by week 3.
Ignoring platform format differences and pasting the same caption length everywhere.
Not checking the closing summary table, missing a skewed mix until after the month is written.
lessons.proTip: Re-run this prompt monthly with 'do not repeat these post concepts: [paste last month's themes]' pasted in, so your calendar keeps evolving instead of cycling the same handful of ideas.

lessons.title: Analyze competitor messaging with Gemini Deep Research before you write
lessons.summary: Use Gemini Deep Research (or ChatGPT Deep Research) to research how competitors actually position themselves right now, with cited sources, so your own positioning is built on current facts instead of stale assumptions.
lessons.goal: Produce a sourced summary of 3-5 competitors' current positioning, pricing signals, and messaging gaps you can exploit.
lessons.whyItMatters: Positioning built on outdated or assumed knowledge of competitors is a common, avoidable mistake — a competitor's pricing, tagline, or main claim can change within a quarter. A Deep Research pass before writing a brief or ad campaign means your differentiation claims are accurate today, not based on what you remember from a year ago, and gives you a cited report you can actually check.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A list of 3-5 real competitor names or URLs. Have a Gemini account (Deep Research is free on the Flash tier; Google AI Pro, about $19.99/mo, raises the quota and uses the stronger Gemini 3.1 Pro model) or a ChatGPT Plus account (about 10 Deep Research runs per month) — either works for this.
steps: Open Gemini (or ChatGPT) and start a Deep Research session rather than a normal chat — this triggers genuine multi-step web research instead of a single-pass answer.
List the specific competitors you want researched by name — vague categories like 'competitors in this space' produce weak results.
Review the research plan Deep Research proposes before it runs, and adjust it if it's missing a competitor or angle you care about.
Wait for the report — Deep Research browses many sources over several minutes to longer, unlike an instant chat reply.
Read the cited report, then cross-check any surprising or important claim by opening the linked source yourself before using it in a brief.
Ask a follow-up in the same session for a short synthesis: where do all competitors sound the same (a saturated claim to avoid) and where is there a clear gap.
Feed the synthesis directly into your campaign brief's positioning statement as grounding evidence.
lessons.prompt:
Research the current public positioning of these competitors: [LIST 3-5 COMPETITOR NAMES OR URLS]. For each one, find and cite sources for: (1) their current homepage headline/tagline, (2) their primary claimed differentiator, (3) any visible pricing or plan structure, (4) one specific claim or proof point they lead with (award, customer count, guarantee, etc.).

Then answer directly: (a) which claims or angles do 2+ of these competitors share (a saturated claim I should avoid repeating), and (b) what does none of them clearly claim or address, that could be a real gap for [MY PRODUCT/CATEGORY]. Cite a source for every factual claim about a competitor — do not state anything about them you can't source.
lessons.explanation: Naming real competitors and requiring a citation for every factual claim is what makes this research trustworthy enough to build a positioning claim on — an unsourced 'Competitor X focuses on enterprise clients' is a guess dressed as a fact, and Deep Research's multi-step web browsing (it visits many sources over several minutes, not a single instant search) is what turns that guess into something checkable, with real cited links in the final report. Explicitly asking what competitors are NOT saying reframes the research from 'copy what works' to 'find the open space,' which is the more useful output for genuine differentiation.
lessons.example:
Input: 3 competing project management tools.

Output: a per-competitor summary — e.g. "Competitor A's homepage headline is [X], sourced from [URL, retrieved date]; their primary differentiator claim is speed of setup" — followed by a synthesis noting that all three competitors lead with 'ease of use' (a saturated claim) and none explicitly addresses agency-specific billing workflows (a possible gap).
lessons.exercise: In your own Gemini or ChatGPT account, run this as a Deep Research brief on 3 real competitors in your category. Open at least one cited source yourself to confirm the claim before using it anywhere.
lessons.expectedResult: A sourced competitor summary with at least one identified saturated claim to avoid and one identified messaging gap, both traceable to real, current sources.
commonMistakes: Asking about 'competitors in general' instead of naming specific companies, which produces vague, unsourced generalizations.
Treating Deep Research like an instant chat reply and not giving it the several minutes it needs to browse and cite real sources.
Using a claim about a competitor in a brief or ad without opening the cited source to confirm it's accurate and current.
Only looking for what competitors claim, and skipping the more useful question of what none of them address.
lessons.proTip: Ask a follow-up specifically for each competitor's negative reviews or common customer complaints (with sources) — that's often a more reliable source of real differentiation than their own marketing claims.

lessons.title: Repurpose one source asset into ten distinct formats
lessons.summary: Turn a single long-form asset — a webinar transcript, blog post, or case study — into ten genuinely distinct pieces of content across formats and platforms, without just chopping it into smaller pieces.
lessons.goal: Produce ten repurposed content pieces from one source asset, each reformatted for its platform's actual conventions rather than just shortened.
lessons.whyItMatters: The lazy version of repurposing — pasting the same three sentences into every platform — reads as spam and performs badly everywhere. Real repurposing extracts a different single idea for each piece and reshapes it to how people actually consume that specific format, which is what lets one piece of source research or content generate a week or more of genuinely useful output instead of one asset stretched thin.
lessons.beforeYouStart: One finished long-form asset: a transcript, article, case study, or report.
steps: Read (or re-skim) the source asset yourself first and note 3-4 distinct standout ideas, quotes, or data points — don't rely on the model to find the best material unsupervised.

Decide which ten formats you actually need (e.g. LinkedIn post, Twitter/X thread, Instagram carousel outline, email newsletter blurb, YouTube Short script, quote graphic caption, FAQ snippet, blog pull-quote, sales one-pager bullet, internal Slack summary).
Paste the source asset plus your list of formats and standout ideas into the prompt, and require each output to be built around a different idea, not the same one restated.
Generate all ten in one pass so you can compare them side by side for redundancy before publishing anything.

Check each piece against its platform's actual convention (thread structure, carousel slide breaks, short-form video hook-in-3-seconds) rather than accepting a generic paragraph reformatted with line breaks.
Schedule the ten pieces across 1-2 weeks rather than posting them all on the same day, so they don't visibly cannibalize each other's reach.
lessons.prompt:
You are a content repurposing specialist. Below is a source asset and a list of standout ideas from it. Produce 10 distinct pieces of content, one per format listed, following platform conventions (not just a shortened paragraph):

Formats needed: [LIST YOUR 10 FORMATS, e.g. LinkedIn post, X/Twitter thread (5-7 tweets), Instagram carousel outline (6-8 slides with slide-by-slide text), email newsletter blurb (80 words), YouTube Short script (150 words, hook in first line), quote graphic caption, FAQ snippet, blog pull-quote, one-pager bullet, internal team summary]

Source asset: [PASTE FULL TEXT OR TRANSCRIPT]
Standout ideas to build from (use a different one as the anchor for each piece, don't reuse the same idea twice): [LIST 3-5 IDEAS/QUOTES/STATS YOU IDENTIFIED]

For each piece, label which standout idea it's built around, then write the content following that platform's actual format conventions. If two pieces would end up nearly identical, choose a different angle from the source instead.
lessons.explanation: Requiring each of the ten pieces to be labeled with the specific idea it's built around is what prevents the classic repurposing failure of ten reformatted copies of the same paragraph — it forces genuine variety at the idea level, not just the format level. Naming actual platform conventions (a 3-second hook for short-form video, slide-by-slide breaks for a carousel) instead of asking for a generic shortened version is what makes each piece feel native to where it's published instead of obviously recycled.
lessons.example:
Source: a 40-minute webinar transcript on remote team management, with standout ideas including a stat on meeting overload, a client quote about async work, and a 3-step framework mentioned mid-talk.

Output: the LinkedIn post built around the meeting-overload stat, the Twitter/X thread built around the 3-step framework broken into one tweet per step, the Instagram carousel built around the client quote as a customer story — each visibly a different piece, not the same summary three times.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, take one real long-form asset you already have and generate ten repurposed pieces using this prompt. Confirm at least 4 different standout ideas were used as anchors across the ten.
lessons.expectedResult: Ten pieces of content that read as native to their platform, built around at least 3-4 different core ideas from the source rather than one idea repeated ten times.
commonMistakes: Letting the model paraphrase the same one or two sentences across most of the ten pieces instead of drawing from multiple distinct ideas in the source.
Accepting a generic shortened paragraph for platforms with real format conventions (threads, carousels, Shorts) instead of asking for the actual native structure.
Publishing all ten pieces on the same day, which visibly competes for the same audience's attention instead of extending reach over time.
Skipping your own read of the source and trusting the model to find the best material unsupervised, which tends to surface the most generic points rather than the most distinctive ones.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running library of past standout ideas already repurposed from each source asset, and paste that list into future repurposing prompts with 'do not reuse these angles' so a single popular asset can keep generating fresh content over months without repeating itself.

lessons.title: Turn a brief into three genuinely distinct first-draft directions
lessons.summary: Use Claude or ChatGPT to generate three meaningfully different first-draft directions from one creative brief, so you're choosing between real options instead of editing a single default draft.
lessons.goal: Produce three distinct first-draft directions from a single brief, each using a different structural or tonal approach.
lessons.whyItMatters: A single AI first draft anchors your thinking around whatever approach the model happened to default to, which is often the most generic option. Asking for three deliberately different directions up front — before you commit to editing anything — gives you real creative options to bring to a client or your own judgment, and takes the same few minutes as generating one flat draft.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A creative brief or project notes: what's being written, for whom, in what format, and any must-include facts.
steps: Gather your brief essentials: format, audience, key message, must-include facts, and word count or length limit.
Ask explicitly for three directions that differ in structure or approach, not just wording — name the three approaches yourself if you already have instincts about them.
Generate all three in one pass so you can compare them side by side.
Read all three once through without editing anything, and note which single one earns a place before touching any of them.
Identify the strongest element across all three (a line, a structure, an opening) even if it's not in your favorite draft.
Pick one direction as your base and, if useful, graft in the strongest element you noticed from another.
lessons.prompt:
You are a copywriter working from the brief below. Write three genuinely distinct first-draft directions for [DELIVERABLE, e.g. a product email, a homepage hero, a 60-second video script]. The three directions must differ in structural approach, not just wording — for example: Direction 1: lead with a story/scenario. Direction 2: lead with a direct claim/promise. Direction 3: lead with a question or provocation.

Brief: format [X], audience [X], key message [X], must-include facts [X], length [X].

Write each direction as a complete draft, not an outline. Label each with its structural approach in one line before the copy. Do not let all three converge on the same opening line or same core sentence reused with different wording.
lessons.explanation: Naming the three structural approaches explicitly (story-led, claim-led, question-led, or whatever fits the format) is what forces real divergence — an unstructured 'give me three versions' request reliably produces three drafts with the same bones and different adjectives. Requiring complete drafts rather than outlines means you're evaluating actual prose and rhythm, which is where most copy decisions really get made, not abstract structure.
lessons.example:
Brief: a product launch email for a new productivity app feature, key message: it saves users 2 hours/week on manual scheduling.

Output: Direction 1 opens with a relatable morning scheduling scenario before naming the feature; Direction 2 opens with a direct claim ("Get 2 hours back every week") and proof; Direction 3 opens with a provocative question ("What would you do with 2 extra hours a week?") — three drafts that would genuinely read as different choices to a client, not one draft in three costumes.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, run this prompt on a real brief you're working from. Pick your base direction and name, in one sentence, why it beat the other two.
lessons.expectedResult: Three complete, structurally distinct drafts where you can articulate a real reason for choosing one over the others, rather than picking whichever came first.
commonMistakes: Accepting three drafts that all open with the same sentence or idea reworded, which isn't real variety.
Asking for outlines instead of full drafts, which hides tone and rhythm problems that only show up in actual prose.
Editing the first direction before reading all three, which anchors your judgment on whichever one you saw first.
Picking a favorite direction without checking whether a stronger individual line or opening exists in one of the other two.
lessons.proTip: Save the two directions you didn't pick — a rejected direction for one project is often exactly the right opening for a different project later, and regenerating from scratch each time wastes a genuinely useful idea.

lessons.title: Edit and tighten any text without losing the writer's voice
lessons.summary: Use targeted editing prompts to cut length and tighten prose while explicitly preserving the original writer's voice, instead of producing a technically shorter but flattened rewrite.
lessons.goal: Cut a piece of text to a target length or tightness while keeping it recognizably in the original writer's voice.
lessons.whyItMatters: The default AI edit tightens by flattening — cutting personality along with the fat, so a distinctive client or brand voice comes back sounding like generic corporate copy. Copywriters get hired specifically for voice, so an editing process that protects it while still cutting real length is the difference between a client trusting AI-assisted editing and a client banning it after one flattened draft.
steps: Paste 2-3 short samples of the actual target voice (the writer's or the brand's own past copy) before asking for any edit — this is the anchor the model needs.
State the specific problem with the current draft: too long, too formal, repetitive, weak opening — not just 'make it better.'
Set a concrete target: word count, or 'cut by X%,' not a vague 'tighten this up.'
Ask explicitly what NOT to change: specific phrases, structure, or facts that must survive the edit untouched.
Compare the edited version against the voice samples line by line, not just for length.
If it drifted toward generic phrasing, name the specific generic phrase and ask for one more targeted pass, not a full rewrite.
lessons.prompt:
You are editing the draft below to cut it to approximately [TARGET WORD COUNT / % SHORTER] while keeping it in the exact voice shown in these writing samples from the same writer/brand:

Voice samples: [PASTE 2-3 SHORT SAMPLES OF THE REAL VOICE]

Draft to edit: [PASTE DRAFT]

Specific problems to fix: [e.g. "too long," "repeats the same point in paragraphs 2 and 4," "opening is weak"]
Do not change: [e.g. "the core facts," "the closing line," "the product name usage"]

Cut length primarily by removing redundant sentences and weak qualifiers, not by shortening or simplifying the sentences that carry the actual voice or personality. Keep sentence rhythm and any distinctive phrasing patterns visible in the voice samples.
lessons.explanation: Pasting real voice samples turns 'keep the voice' from a vague instruction into a concrete target the model can pattern-match against, which is the difference between an edit that sounds like the original writer and one that sounds like a competent stranger. Naming the specific problem (repetition, weak opening) instead of asking for a generic tightening pass focuses the cut on what's actually wrong, and explicitly protecting sentence rhythm — not just facts — is what stops the flattening effect where every edit converges toward the same neutral, safe phrasing.
lessons.example:
Draft: a 220-word brand blog intro with a distinctive, slightly irreverent voice, target: cut to 140 words.

A naive tightening pass would likely strip the irreverent asides as 'unnecessary' along with genuine filler. With voice samples pasted in and 'keep sentence rhythm and distinctive phrasing' specified, the edit instead removes a redundant second explanation of the same point and a throat-clearing opening sentence, while keeping the voice's characteristic short punchy sentences and one signature aside intact.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, edit a real draft down by at least 30% using this prompt, with real voice samples pasted in. Read the result against the original voice samples and flag anything that now sounds generic.
lessons.expectedResult: A version that is meaningfully shorter and reads as written by the same person or brand, with at least one distinctive phrasing pattern from the voice samples still present.
commonMistakes: Asking for a tighter draft with no voice samples, which reliably produces competent but flattened, generic prose.
Requesting 'make it shorter' without naming what's actually wrong, so the model cuts randomly instead of removing the real redundancy.
Not specifying what must stay unchanged, resulting in an edit that accidentally cuts a key fact or the intended closing line.
Accepting the edit without comparing it back against the voice samples, missing a drift toward generic corporate phrasing.
lessons.proTip: Build a standing 'voice sample' snippet for each regular client or brand and keep it saved somewhere you can paste from instantly — voice-anchored edits only work if pulling up real samples takes seconds, not a search through old files.

lessons.title: Build a headline system: generate, score, and shortlist
lessons.summary: Generate a large, varied headline set using named headline formulas, then score and shortlist systematically instead of picking by gut feel from an unstructured list.
lessons.goal: Produce 15-20 headlines built from distinct, named formulas, scored against clear criteria, and shortlisted to a defensible top 3.
lessons.whyItMatters: An unstructured 'give me 15 headlines' request produces a list where most entries are minor rewordings of one or two ideas, and picking a winner comes down to gut feel that's hard to explain to a client. Generating from named formulas and scoring against explicit criteria produces real variety and a shortlist you can justify in a client meeting instead of just asserting a favorite.
steps: Have the core message or benefit ready in one plain sentence before generating any headlines.
Ask for headlines built from named formulas (benefit-led, curiosity-led, number/specificity-led, direct-address, problem-led) rather than an unstructured list.
Generate 3-4 headlines per formula so you get real coverage of each approach.
Ask for a score against explicit criteria — clarity, specificity, and whether it would stop a scroll or skim.
Read the scored list and sanity-check the top 5 yourself; scoring is a filter, not a final decision.
Shortlist 3 finalists from at least 2 different formulas, not all from the highest-scoring category alone.
lessons.prompt:
You are a headline specialist. The core message is: [ONE PLAIN SENTENCE — THE ACTUAL BENEFIT OR CLAIM]. Audience: [X]. Format: [e.g. blog title, email subject line, ad headline — specify length limit if relevant].

Generate 4 headlines for each of these 5 formulas (20 total):
1. Benefit-led (states the outcome directly)
2. Curiosity-led (creates an open loop without clickbait)
3. Number/specificity-led (uses a real specific detail, not an invented stat)
4. Direct-address (speaks straight to the reader's situation)
5. Problem-led (names the pain before the solution)

Then score every headline 1-5 on: clarity (is the point instantly clear), specificity (concrete detail vs. vague claim), and scroll-stop (would this interrupt a skim). Show the scores in a table. Do not invent a statistic or claim not supported by: [PASTE ANY REAL FACTS/NUMBERS AVAILABLE].
lessons.explanation: Naming the five formulas up front is what produces headlines that are structurally different from each other rather than the same idea in different words, which is the most common failure of open-ended headline brainstorms. Scoring against three concrete, named criteria — rather than an overall vague 'quality' score — makes the shortlist defensible: you can point to exactly why a headline scored well instead of just asserting a preference, which matters directly when presenting options to a client.
lessons.example:
Core message: this budgeting app finds an average of $200/month in unused subscriptions.

Output: benefit-led ("Find the $200 a month you didn't know you were losing"), curiosity-led ("The subscription costing you $200 a month, hiding in plain sight"), number-led using the real $200 figure rather than inventing a bigger one, direct-address ("You're probably paying for something you forgot about"), problem-led ("Stop paying for subscriptions you don't use") — each scored on clarity, specificity, and scroll-stop, with the top 3 shortlisted from at least two different formulas.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, run this prompt with a real headline you're working on. Shortlist 3 finalists from at least 2 different formulas and note the one score that most influenced each choice.
lessons.expectedResult: A 20-headline set with visible structural variety across formulas, a scored table, and a 3-headline shortlist you can justify with specific reasoning rather than gut feel.
commonMistakes: Skipping the named formulas and getting 20 headlines that are mostly rewordings of the same one or two ideas.
Letting the model invent a bigger or more impressive stat than the one you actually have.
Trusting the scores as a final ranking instead of a filter, and skipping your own sanity check on the top results.
Shortlisting all three finalists from the single highest-scoring formula, losing the point of testing genuinely different approaches.
lessons.proTip: Keep a log of which formula type actually wins in real tests for your specific audience over time — after a dozen campaigns you'll often find one or two formulas reliably outperform for that audience, which should shift how many headlines you generate from each formula going forward.

lessons.title: Write research-backed copy: gather verifiable facts before you draft
lessons.summary: Use ChatGPT Deep Research to gather sourced, checkable facts and data points before writing, so your copy's claims are accurate and defensible instead of vague or invented.
lessons.goal: Produce a short, sourced fact sheet on a topic before drafting copy, so every specific claim in the final copy traces back to a real, checkable source.
lessons.whyItMatters: Copy that makes specific claims — a statistic, an industry trend, a comparison — is stronger than vague copy, but only if the claims are true; an invented or misremembered stat that gets challenged by a client or a reader damages trust fast. A Deep Research pass before drafting turns 'studies show...' into a specific, sourced, and checkable fact, and separating research from drafting keeps the writing step from quietly inventing numbers under deadline pressure.
lessons.beforeYouStart: The topic or claim area your copy needs to reference (an industry stat, a trend, a comparison point). Have a ChatGPT Plus account or higher — Deep Research isn't available on the Free or Go tiers, and Plus includes about 10 Deep Research runs per month, so save them for claims that really matter.
steps: Identify the 2-4 specific factual claims your copy would be stronger for having — not 'research the topic' broadly, but the actual claims you want to make.
In ChatGPT, select Deep Research in the composer and submit the claims as a research brief, requiring a cited, checkable source for every answer.
Answer any clarifying questions ChatGPT asks before it starts researching — this shapes what it actually goes and searches for.
Wait for the report to finish — Deep Research browses many sources over several minutes to longer, it isn't an instant chat reply.
Open at least the most important cited source yourself to confirm it says what the summary claims it says.
Note the exact source and date next to each fact so you can cite it later or defend it if a client asks.
Only then move to drafting, writing the specific sourced fact into the copy rather than a vague paraphrase.
If no good source exists for a claim you wanted to make, cut the claim or replace it with a softer, honest phrasing rather than keeping a specific number you can't back.
lessons.prompt:
Research the following claims and find current, citable sources for each. Do not state anything as fact without a source; if you cannot find a reliable source for a claim, say so explicitly instead of guessing.

Claims to research: [LIST 2-4 SPECIFIC CLAIMS, e.g. "average time small businesses spend on invoicing per month," "industry adoption rate of X in 2025-2026," "typical cost difference between X and Y"]
Context: [WHAT THE COPY IS FOR AND WHO IT'S FOR]

For each claim, give: the specific fact/figure, the source name and URL, and the publication or data date. Flag anything more than 2 years old as potentially outdated. Then suggest one sentence of copy for each fact, written as a direct, specific claim (not vague language like 'studies show') with the source figure embedded naturally.
lessons.explanation: Separating research from drafting — and explicitly instructing the model to say 'no reliable source found' rather than guess — is the core anti-hallucination guardrail here; a drafting-only prompt under deadline pressure will often produce a plausible-sounding but unsupported number because that's what completes the sentence best, not because it's true. ChatGPT's Deep Research mode browses many real sources over several minutes rather than answering from memory in one pass, which is what makes the citations checkable. Flagging source age matters because a genuinely accurate but three-year-old statistic can still mislead a reader into thinking it reflects the current market.
lessons.example:
Claim to research: "average small business spends significant time monthly on manual invoicing."

Output: a specific figure with a named source and date (e.g. a named industry survey, 2025), flagged as current, followed by a suggested copy line embedding the real figure directly rather than the vague original phrasing — or, if no solid source turns up, an explicit note that the claim isn't well supported and a suggested honest rephrase instead.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account (Plus or higher), run this as a Deep Research brief on 2-3 real claims you want to use in upcoming copy. Open at least one source yourself before writing the claim into any draft.
lessons.expectedResult: A short fact sheet where every claim has a named, dated source you've personally verified for at least the most important item, ready to write directly into copy.
commonMistakes: Asking for research too broadly ('tell me about this industry') instead of naming the specific claims you actually want to make.
Writing a sourced-sounding claim into copy without opening the actual source to confirm it says what the summary implies.
Using a stat that's several years old without flagging or checking whether it still reflects the current market.
Keeping a specific invented-sounding number in the final copy when no real source was ever found for it, instead of softening the claim honestly.
lessons.proTip: Deep Research runs are limited (about 10/month on Plus), so save them for claims that really matter; for recurring topics (an industry you write about often), keep a running, dated fact sheet you update every few months instead of re-researching from zero on every project — but always re-verify dates before reusing an old fact in new copy.

lessons.title: Apply client revision rounds fast and consistently
lessons.summary: Turn scattered client feedback into a structured, trackable revision pass so every note gets addressed accurately in one round instead of triggering three more rounds of miscommunication.
lessons.goal: Apply a full set of client feedback notes to a draft in one accurate pass, with a clear record of what changed and why.
lessons.whyItMatters: Client feedback often arrives as a mix of vague notes ('make it punchier'), contradictory requests, and specific line edits, and applying it inconsistently is what turns one revision round into four. Structuring the feedback before applying it — separating specific asks from vague ones, flagging contradictions instead of silently picking one — produces a revision the client recognizes as responsive and a change log you can point to if they ask what moved.
steps: Collect all client feedback in one place, even if it came from multiple emails or comments, before touching the draft.
Sort the feedback into specific asks (a named line, a named change) versus vague direction ('make it punchier,' 'more premium feel') before applying anything.
Flag any two notes that contradict each other and get a call on the real intent rather than guessing silently.
Apply specific asks exactly as stated first, since those are unambiguous.
Apply vague direction only after specific asks are handled, translating it into concrete changes and naming what you changed to satisfy it.
Generate a short change log mapping each feedback note to what was actually changed, so the client can verify their notes were addressed.
lessons.prompt:
You are revising the draft below based on client feedback. Separate the feedback into (a) specific asks and (b) vague/directional notes before applying anything. If any two notes contradict each other, list the contradiction explicitly instead of silently choosing one.

Original draft: [PASTE DRAFT]
Client feedback (paste as given, even if messy): [PASTE ALL FEEDBACK]

Apply the specific asks first, exactly as stated. Then address each vague note with a concrete change, and state in one line what you changed to satisfy it (e.g. "'more premium feel' → replaced three casual contractions and shortened the closing paragraph"). End with a change log: one line per feedback note, mapping it to the specific change made. Do not make any change not traceable to a feedback note or a contradiction you flagged.
lessons.explanation: Splitting specific asks from vague direction before applying anything prevents the two most common revision failures: overcorrecting on a vague note while missing a precise one buried in the same email, and silently resolving a contradiction in a way the client didn't actually intend. The mandatory change log is what makes the revision defensible — a client who says 'this doesn't feel like what I asked for' can be shown exactly which note produced which change, turning a vague disagreement into a specific, resolvable one.
lessons.example:
Feedback: "Love the opening. Can we cut this down by half? Also make the CTA stronger. And can it feel a bit more premium — actually maybe keep it casual, our audience is pretty relaxed."

Output: flags the contradiction between 'more premium' and 'keep it casual' explicitly rather than picking one silently, applies the clear specific ask (cut by half, stronger CTA) first, and asks for clarification on the tone note before finalizing that part — with a change log line for each addressed item.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, apply a real (or realistic) set of mixed client feedback to a draft using this prompt. Check the change log against the original feedback to confirm nothing was missed or invented.
lessons.expectedResult: A revised draft with every specific ask applied exactly, vague notes translated into named concrete changes, any real contradiction flagged rather than silently resolved, and a change log the client could read and recognize.
commonMistakes: Applying feedback in the order it was written instead of specific-first, which sometimes lets a vague note override a precise one.
Silently picking a resolution to contradictory feedback instead of flagging it back to the client or account lead.
Skipping the change log, which makes it harder to prove a note was actually addressed when a client claims it wasn't.
Making unrequested 'improvements' alongside the actual feedback, which muddies what changed and why and can reopen settled decisions.
lessons.proTip: When feedback is genuinely vague ('punchier,' 'more premium'), ask the client for one example of writing that already hits that feel before revising — a single reference point turns a subjective note into something you can pattern-match against directly.

lessons.title: Build your personal style guide as a reusable prompt asset
lessons.summary: Turn your own writing patterns into a structured style guide you can paste into any prompt, so every AI-assisted draft starts already sounding like you instead of generic.
lessons.goal: Produce a structured, reusable style-guide document from your own past writing that you can paste into future prompts to anchor tone and voice automatically.
lessons.whyItMatters: Copywriters who use AI well aren't the ones with the cleverest single prompt — they're the ones who've turned their own voice into a reusable asset, so every new project starts from 'sounds like me' instead of 'sounds like a competent stranger.' A real style guide, built from your actual writing rather than adjectives you'd use to describe yourself, is the single highest-leverage asset for making AI drafts consistently usable without heavy editing.
lessons.beforeYouStart: 5-10 samples of your own best writing across a few different formats (emails, headlines, longer pieces).
steps: Gather 5-10 samples of writing you consider genuinely representative of your best, most distinctive work — not your average output.
Ask the model to analyze the samples for concrete, checkable patterns (sentence length variation, favorite structures, punctuation habits, what you avoid) rather than vague adjectives.
Push back on any vague trait it names ('conversational,' 'engaging') by asking for the specific mechanism that creates that impression.
Organize the findings into a structured guide: sentence patterns, vocabulary/word choices to use and avoid, structural habits, and 3-5 signature moves.
Test the guide immediately by pasting it into a fresh prompt for a new piece and checking whether the output actually sounds like you.
Revise the guide based on what the test draft got wrong, then save it as a standing snippet you paste into every future drafting prompt.
lessons.prompt:
Analyze the writing samples below and build a personal style guide. Do not use vague adjectives alone (e.g. 'conversational,' 'punchy') — for every trait you name, identify the specific mechanism that creates it (e.g. sentence length pattern, punctuation choice, a specific word class used or avoided) with a quoted example from the samples.

Writing samples: [PASTE 5-10 SAMPLES OF YOUR OWN BEST WRITING]

Produce a style guide with these sections:
1. Sentence patterns (typical length, rhythm, how variation is used — with quoted examples)
2. Vocabulary habits (words/phrasing you favor, words you avoid, quoted examples of both)
3. Structural habits (how pieces typically open and close, use of lists/short paragraphs, etc.)
4. Signature moves (3-5 specific techniques that appear repeatedly and feel distinctive to this writer, each with a quoted example)
5. A short paste-ready instruction block I can drop into future prompts to write in this voice, under 100 words, built only from the patterns above.
lessons.explanation: Forcing every trait to trace back to a specific, quotable mechanism instead of a vague adjective is what makes the resulting guide actually usable — 'write conversationally' means almost nothing to a model, but 'favor short declarative sentences and one long sentence with a semicolon per paragraph, avoid corporate hedges like "in order to"' is something it can pattern-match against reliably. The final paste-ready instruction block is the actual deliverable: a compact, reusable asset rather than a document you'd have to re-read and re-summarize every time.
lessons.example:
Input: 6 samples of a writer's emails and blog posts with a habit of short punchy openers followed by one longer explanatory sentence, and a near-total avoidance of exclamation points and corporate phrases like 'reach out.'

Output: a guide naming 'opens with a 4-8 word declarative sentence, followed by one longer sentence that explains or complicates it' as a signature move, with two quoted examples, plus a paste-ready 80-word instruction block summarizing all of it for future prompts.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, build a real style guide from your own past writing. Paste the final instruction block into a prompt for a new, unrelated piece and check whether a colleague could tell it was styled after you.
lessons.expectedResult: A style guide where every trait is backed by a quoted example from your real writing, plus a compact instruction block that, when pasted into a new prompt, measurably shifts the output toward your actual voice rather than a generic default.
commonMistakes: Accepting vague adjective-only trait descriptions ('friendly,' 'professional') that give the model nothing concrete to pattern-match against.
Building the guide from average or rushed writing samples instead of your genuinely best, most distinctive work.
Never testing the guide on a real new draft, so an inaccurate or incomplete pattern goes uncaught.
Letting the instruction block grow long and vague instead of staying tight and specific enough to actually paste into every prompt without friction.
lessons.proTip: Rebuild this guide roughly once a year, or after any deliberate shift in how you write — a style guide built from writing you did two years ago will quietly steer new drafts back toward an older version of your voice.
